newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr backs off highs, wages a mixed bag.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr backs off highs, wages a mixed bag.

text.p: The Australian dollar hung onto much of Wednesday's hefty gains at the midsession as the market wondered what mixed Q1 wages data meant for interest rates.
On the face of it a downward revsion in annual weekly earnings growth to 4.3 percent from 4.6 percent would seemed to have increased the chance of an easing.
However, the breakdown confounded expectations by showing private sector wage growth accelerated by 1.3 percent in the quarter while public sector growth slowed sharply.
This had to be a blow to the easing camp which had based their case on expectations of subdued private sector wages.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the currency had pulled back to US$0.7830/35 having romped as high as US$0.7888 overnight in an explosive short covering rally.
That was still well up on Wednesday's late US$0.7761/66 and far above its trough of US$0.7713.

It was also broadly higher on the crosses as bears bailed out of short positions established in the anticipation of a U.S. rate hike which never came. The local dollar was up at 90.02/12 yen from 88.15/25 late Wednesday and at 59.4 in trade weighted terms from just 58.6 yesterday.
A further rally in US$/yen contributed to the firmer tone.

Dealers said Japanese demand for US$/yen had been apparent this morning, probably encouraged by surprisingly favourable U.S. trade data overnight, pushing the dollar to 114.92/02 yen from 114.32/37 in New York and 113.60/70 this time Wednesday.
On the domestic front a small but vocal group in the market had been touting today's final wages data as the factor which would tip the Reserve Bank's hand toward easing.

They got part of what they wanted in that annual growth in overall average weekly earnings was revised down to 4.3 percent from 4.6 percent. It was therefore below the 4.5 percent level which the RBA has often expressed unease with in the past.

However, their argument had been that aggregate wages growth was biased upwards by special circumstances in the public sector and private sector pay deals, which are far more important for inflation, were running at lower levels and not a danger.
In fact private sector wages grew 1.3 percent in the quarter almost twice the pace of the 0.7 percent public rise.
The annual rate shifted to 3.6 percent which, while still well beneath public sector growth of 7.1 percent, was a significant acceleration from the 2.8 percent held in Q4.
Analysts said it was an open question whether the rise was the start of an upward trend and some felt strongly it was not.
However, it would be hard to be certain about the trend until the next quarterly wages release and that was not due until August.

If the RBA decided to wait for confirmation and the economy showed clear signs of a pick up by then, as the bank itself expects, then it might well be reluctant to make a pro-cyclical easing, analysts said.
